newsitem.title: BELGIUM: BELGIUM MAY DROP STATE GUARANTEE FOR HWI MONEY BROKER.
newsitem.headline: BELGIUM MAY DROP STATE GUARANTEE FOR HWI MONEY BROKER.

text.p: The Belgian government is considering dropping the state guarantee given to the Inter Dealer Broker activity of HWI-IRG, a semi-official money broker, Belgian Finance Minister Philippe Maystadt said on Wednesday.

"I have asked my cabinet to study whether the state guarantee is still needed. The state could, in a near future, withdraw the guarantee given to the IRG-HWI for the market activities of the institute," Maystadt told the finance commission of Belgian parliament.
He was replying to questions by Green party Agalev parliament member Jef Tavernier.
The IRG-HWI is owned by Belgian banks but some of its board members are appointed by the government and its commitments are guaranteed by the state.

In recent years, the institute -- originaly set up as a bank deposit guarantor, a function it still performs -- has become a major force in the Belgian money market. It acts as an anonymous counterparty in the Treasury bill market and is also very active in the repo market.
"The state guarantee has become less essential today as financial markets have become very competitive and liquid," Maystadt said in a speech to the parliamentary commission.
"(The guarantee) also risks breaching European guidelines on free competition and state aid to companies," he added.
Maystadt said that HWI-IRG is an important player in the money market and said the institute boosted transparency of secundary markets for government paper.
"It is important that, in periods of tension, all counterparties in the market can count on a credible institution whose first goal is not the pursuit of profit," he said.
HWI director Herman Debremaeker told Reuters that his institution would have no trouble functioning without the state guarantee.
"If that is the minister's opinion, we will subscribe to it," he said, adding that HWI so far never had to use the state guarantee.
In 1995 HWI had trading volume worth 4,500 billion francs, half of it in T-bills, half in repos.
Maystadt and Debremaeker rejected Tavernier's assertion the state was running a large financial risk via the HWI.
"Our activity holds no risk whatsoever for the state," Debremaeker told Reuters.
Tavernier said the loans to banks given via repos (with state bonds as collateral) carried a market risk.
Tavernier told Reuters in parliament that this consisted of the risk that the value of the collateral could depreciate during the life of the repo.
"The risk can hardly deteriorate considering the (short) maturity of the repos," Maystadt said.
Debremaeker said that HWI asks (and gives) extra collateral if the market value of the collateral changes during the life of the repo, which is three weeks on average.

In response to Tavernier's criticism that the HWI was hiding its market exposure through repos, Maystadt said that as of the 1996 financial year, the HWI would start booking repos and reverse repos in its balance sheet.
